p: Yes, I'm going to pass this to Nicole, but I, I'm, I'm glad that you asked that question because as I said, this is a very unique population, the post-9/11 veterans. We are at a point where, um, this is one of the most diverse generations um, one of the most educated generations too. Um, so the simple fact of us, um, at the moment of having these conversations is very important. I know that, for example, Council, uh, Member, when you came to the roundtable, um, I know we were only able to touch up on mental health and we didn't even finish on the whole mental health situation, but there's, uh, it— there's different issues that need to be approached, differently. Uh, but I know, as DVS, I'm still continue having these conversations. I'm still not done having the roundtables on the post-9/11, uh, veterans, um, which all of you will also be invited. But I'll pass on this question to Nicole.

Thank you, Chair. For us, it's also important to notice that we know our veterans

are in the community. So if they're not identifying to us, we know that they're in each City Council district. And I think we had this conversation previously too where we do hold this data for which veterans are in each council district. So we encourage all Council Members to connect with us to get that data of which veterans are in their districts so that more of that direct community building and outreach can be done. I think additionally with us in that spirit of partnership is that we're really excited to partner with different organizations, as Council Member Paladino said, that may not be veteran-oriented but can help support veterans, especially when we're thinking about in super local areas and on that level. I know that in the Veterans Advisory Report, and there has been discourse around our part in promoting candidate— veteran candidates and things of that nature. And while that's something that we are not exploring, what we do are in support of is veterans increasing their civic engagement and really being able to be involved on that local level.

Thank you. Um, Commissioner, the— I, I don't have any interest in using this forum, um, to push any partisan political agenda or anything like that. So I'm not trying to insert you in any sort of political controversy, uh, but I do have to ask you about this, not only because you're the Commissioner, but because you're a post-9/11 veteran yourself. Um, Mayor Adams last year, eh, announced that, uh, this coming July there would be a ticker tape parade. He called it the Homecoming of Heroes to honor post-9/11 combat veterans and their families. It was announced, uh, last week, uh, that Mayor Mamdani is not gonna go forward with that. I'm wondering if you could speak at all to what your understanding was of the circumstances behind that decision and what the Administration may be considering in terms of honoring the post-9/11 veterans.

Yes, thank you for that question, Council Member. So as uh, as DVS, we have been having various meetings. As I mentioned, I've had close to 100 meetings and we are listening directly from, uh, the veterans themselves. There have been

various, um, conversations of different things that, that, that have been said, whether it has been a ruck, whether it's been a resource fair. So what we, and what we then did was then convene the, a meeting, uh, most recently as well about the, with the post-9/11 veterans. And when it comes to that, we are still in organizing the next steps of the ruck and the, um, the resource fair because we, unlike the previous Administration, we want to make sure that the voices of veterans are included and they're the ones that help us shape this and are part of the coordination. Um, so there's still a lot more conversation to come on that, on how we're gonna do the ruck and the resource fair. But just to give an example about the ruck, the ruck is a universal per se, um, language where it doesn't matter what branch you served. The ruck is very universal for us that it's when we put, uh, um, um, about whether it is 30 to 50 pounds in our, in our, in our rucksack and, and would like to maybe keep it simple, but like in March, and it's a way for us to, to pay tribute to whomever it was that we were, that, that we're honoring at that moment.

So as- as that, um, that requires, um, that is very tedious and not easy to do. But when it comes to the resource fair, this is the first time that we're gonna be convening so many, um, veteran groups, nonprofits, all in one space. Um, because we want to make sure that veterans know that we're here for you. It's not just like, uh, a parade, but it's, it's what we want you to know is that we're doing it by action, that we are here to provide those services, that, and, and we do hope that through that, uh, we send that message that we are leading by an example and by action. And again, this is going to require, um, uh, more conversations to have. Like, I know with the post-9/11 convening that we had, we had, uh, a conversation around that. Um, and, and veterans are, are letting us know, like, that you should change this or you should add this. But, um, with that, we are working very closely. I, I believe, um, um, with the Travis Foundation too, to be able to— they've done this ruck so many times, they, they've done the Brooklyn Bridge, and we're going to be working with them to get guidance from them on how to do this, this, this ruck.

So, like, to your point, we've been convening with veteran groups, and they are guiding us in this process, and they're going to be part of every conversation. And we also invite your offices too to be part of this.

Well, thank you. I'm definitely— I appreciate being included and look forward to being part of the conversation. And, and it's fine if you don't, but do you have an understanding of why that decision was made to go in a different direction? Is it a question of resources? Is it a question of police, uh, logistics? Is it something else?

So when it comes to that, what has been, um, as I started convening various veteran groups, um, there has been a, a lot of conversations that many veteran groups were not included in this process. And that is what I do differently. I like to include veterans. I like to hear from them. I like them to be the ones leading this. Um, and also when it does come to funding per se, right? It's, um, it's, it's something that, that as an agency, I'm really looking into as an agency and to see, like, if, if this is something that can

continue every year, because when you plan something, it's not just that it's just for this year, it's a planification process. So I do hope that with the support and, and the guidance, I would like to say, of veterans themselves, that perhaps next year is going to be something else, right? But we need to start from the bottom up, which is like, right now we're gathering with veteran groups. They're letting us know what works, what doesn't work, what they like, what they don't like. And it's not always easy conversations, but that's what part of organizing is. Like, you have to have hard conversations and to make sure that everybody feels part of this. And also, not only will we be honoring those post-9/11 veterans, but we are also going to take the opportunity to have Vietnam veterans there present, because it— again, we can't learn from our present or look forward to the future if we don't know about our past.
Council Member Paladino.

I'm switching topics on you, uh, I want to, uh, delve into our VA hospitals. And, uh, you know, we know the city budget is $5

million for the veterans. We know that our VA hospitals are absolutely disgusting.
Hmm.

Uh, quite frankly, uh, I would like to know, and I would like to ask, uh, how about we do start to do some surprise checks. St. Albans in my borough comes to mind because we happen to know several veterans who had to go to St. Albans.
Mhm.

And, uh, I'd like to know if we could start to do some— be proactive. Out of that $5 million, now we also have a Committee that is hospitals. Okay, called hospitals. Well, how much of their budget actually goes towards our VA hospitals? Hmm, they're a mess. The food— this is— I'm reading right out of one of my vets. The food is gross. The veterans are neglected. No answers for families. Have to be pre-approved— for we, we as elected have to be pre-approved to visit. I cannot walk into a veterans hospital, which is total
Mhm.
Absolute BS that I cannot walk in as a sitting elected who happens to serve on the Veterans Committee and ask to meet with— way I do at my homeless shelters.
Mhm.

I'm very much in touch. So the idea that I'm cut off from that is something that needs to be— tells me, what are you hiding? Because if I can't walk in and say, hello, how are you, ah, without being asked to leave immediately upon my arrival, I find that not only disrespectful, but totally lacking in any kind of confidence, like they're hiding something. Also, these veterans should have access to EBT cards. The way the illegal immigrants in this country have. So I have a problem with that as well. Again, this is coming directly from a veteran. And again, it's gross about how they are treated. Elected officials should be able to walk in at any given times to do random checks. So $5 million, hospitals are a shambles, elected officials cannot just randomly drop in and say hello uh, and EBT cards. So let's keep those 3 on the front burner. That— I'm sorry to shift from such a

nice topic that you were having prior, but I really— I just got this from him, and I really wanted this addressed because again, like I said, the budget for the veterans is disgraceful. I've been sitting on this Committee, this will be 5 years. $5 million hasn't been increased, not by 1 cent. We have Committees here that are— it's a Hospitals Committee. What else? What, what's the Committee called? Hospitals and General Welfare? General Welfare? You would know. Just Hospitals, flat out Hospitals. So how much out of the Hospitals Committee actually goes to are veterans hospitals.
Mhm.
And I wanna be allowed in anytime I wanna go. And I think they should be able to be entitled to EBT cards. That's all. Thank you.

Thank you, Councilwoman, for that question because, um, even though the VA is handled at a federal level, I know that we do have good relationships with the VA and that is something unique that we're doing now, um, er, under my leadership is that I'm trying to build, at least open up that line of communication. And I know that part

of the organizing per se that we would like to do is begin having meetings with the VA directly. And, and this is where we would like to invite you, and so to begin having these conversations.

And on a personal note, my father died in 1961. He died in a VA hospital because my mother could not afford had any other hospitalization for my dad. So he died, like I said, up in the Bronx in, in the VA hospital. So that was many, many, many, many years ago, but it's as current today, mhm, as it was in 1961. This just came to me as I'm— I lost my dad in the VA hospital.

I'm so sorry for that, uh, Councilwoman, and, and, and, and with that, um, that's why we want to make sure that we have good relationships. And I'm— and I can have a follow-up, uh, conversation with you on that, on how we are trying to also, um, team up with the VA hospital. And there's a whole other conversation that we're having with them, but we would like to bring you in that conversation and also, um, further, um, emphasize that what we can do collectively is make sure that— the veterans know the alternative that they have if they're not supported at the—
City Hall has a Hospitals Committee. We- Council, has a Hospitals Committee.
Mhm.

I think you should start there. And let's find out in their line item for the new budget, $127 billion. That's a lot of money. Let's find out how much of that $127 billion that's being allotted to the Hospitals Committee is actually gonna go toward the heroes of this country. I, I'm dead serious about that. Dead, dead serious about that. Thank you.

Thank you. Thank you, Councilwoman and the next— to finalize this, we are trying to build that strong relationship with the Commissioner from DOHMH um, because, um, we would like to have these conversations with them on how can alternatively they can support veterans if the VA is not doing that. So that's another, um, uh, meeting that we're gonna have with the second meeting that we're gonna have with the Commissioner from

Uh, thank you, Council Member, for your family service as well. Uh,

Commissioner, you've given us a lot to think about in your testimony, and, uh, I think one of the things that was most readily apparent is that we should be listening to the voices of veterans, which we're— we'll, we'll do in a moment. Uh, is there anything else you want to leave us with?

I just want to reassure you that as the new Commissioner coming in within my 2 months Uh, we— I am looking very deep into all the data. We are currently even submitting a report, uh, a particular report on disability that had not been submitted for the last 3 years, just so you know. And within my 2 months, we're submitting it and we're convening a roundtable with disability advocates so they could also look at this report and tell us what is wrong or what do we need to change. And also to, um, hold, hold me as an agency accountable, like, well, how is it that they're going to be holding me accountable? I'm all about accountability. So I just want you to know that what we are doing within my agency, like, within my 2 months, again, we are submitting— even, I'm even looking through what reports haven't been submitted. I just want to be transparent about that. So I am making sure that we

are up to date. I am also making sure that with Local Law 37, that that's fully implemented. And also because I want to make sure that the veteran groups here have the most accurate data so they could advocate for their nonprofit and that they're fully supported when it comes to Local Law 37, when they're asking for contracts. And I, I, I always tell my team that we need to be respectful to all the veterans that are here. So we are— we stay, um, and listen to each one of them. So I just want— I want them to know that we're also listening and being fully supportive of them.

When, when I talked about the Hospitals Committee, one way you may be able to finagle yourself around a little bit is look at all our different Committees that we have. And why not delve into the so many— there's how many Committees in the City Council? How many that could actually assist the veterans? Something you should look into because funding does not necessarily have to just be the one allotted amount of $5 million. There's other pots that you should be able to dip into in order to get your money.
Yeah, I, I think that's a great point. If you look at every Committee, which one doesn't have something to do with veterans, you know, General Welfare, Finance, even Criminal Justice. Absolutely.
There's so many ways. Thank you.
Thank you Commissioner. Uh, thank you, everybody. Appreciate your help.
Thank you. Thank you.

Alright, uh, we are now going to open the hearing for public testimony. I want to remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. Uh, the witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. Uh, no video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant-at-Arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you'll have 3 minutes to speak on today's hearing topic, Serving Post-9/11 Veterans. We'll hear all in-person testimony first and then turn to testimony on Zoom. Uh, the members of this Committee may ask you a question or two, uh, but if we don't, that doesn't mean we're not interested. Would trust me when I tell you we're paying very, very close attention to what everybody's saying. If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant-at-Arms. Alright, I will now call the first panel. When you hear your name, come on up. Uh, I will welcome Joseph Wein, Jenny Bucove, Christina Brown Fisher and Coco Culhane, come on down. And if, uh, I do mispronounce anyone's name, please correct me. Alright, uh, thank you. Uh, begin with Mr. Wein, who, uh, in addition to being a Marine veteran, is also, uh, uh, somebody that I've

had the privilege of knowing personally and who gifted me this, um, embassy, uh, panel from the U.S. Embassy in Baghdad, Iraq when he was serving there, and it's, uh, my privilege to wear it. Uh, so thank you, Mr. Wein.

Thank you. Uh, good, good morning, everybody. It's a pleasure to be here. It's a pleasure to be back in this room. Uh, as you'll hear in my statement, I worked in the Council many years ago before I was called back to work. Alright, by work I mean government work, which— this is government work. But good, good morning, Frank, Chairman, uh, and Members of the, uh, Council. It's a pleasure to be here. So I'm proud to say that I'm a native New Yorker, right? Born and raised here. I am equally proud to be a third-generation Marine, combat veteran Marine. And I also like to say that I come from a family of immigrants from Cuba and Italy. Both sides of my family have served in the military since 1914, and that tradition continues today. My nephew is a pilot in the Navy, but I cannot disclose where he is or what type of plane he flies. But I assure you he is in harm's way. Alright, I

joined the Marine Corps immediately after high school, and I served for 4 years on active duty. During that time, I was deployed to the First Gulf War, where I was a scout with the now Second Light Armored Reconnaissance Battalion. I later deployed with the 26th Marine Expeditionary Unit, a special operations capable force, um, which supported Operation Provide Promise in the former Republic of Yugoslavia. And I trained with our partner nations across Europe, Africa, and the Middle East. After returning to New York City, I worked for Council Member Jay O'Donovan, which I don't know if anybody up here remembers him, but he was the first Vietnam vet elected to the Council. Uh, I later ran for City Council myself in the 50th District, and as fate would have it, my primary day was September 11th, 2001. Alright, after, uh, obviously, uh, that kind of threw a wrench into my campaign. I did not win, but I went on to work down at Ground Zero for about a year. Um, after assisting down at Ground Zero, I returned to service with the US Department of State's High Protection Office— High Threat Protection Office.

Uh, I was assigned to the Baghdad, ah, office protecting, uh, diplomatic personnel during Operation Iraqi Freedom. I served there in Iraq from 2005 to 2008, continuous service, coming home occasionally for leave. I later was tasked to work with the USAID, the, and the State Department Security Service again in Afghanistan, where I was there in 2009 and 2010. Upon returning to the United States, I supported, uh, domestic emergency responses and continued, uh, security and leadership roles. Uh, my current role is security sensitive, so I will not give you any specific details of what I do now or who I work for. However, I want to emphasize that the opinions, experience, and perspectives that I share to you today are my own, shaped, and mine alone, are shaped over 55 years of life and service. I share this background to make the point clear: veterans have earned access to the care and support they were promised. The transition from military to civilian life is not an easy one. It’s more difficult for others than some alright, and access to the Department of Veterans Affairs and Services is a critical part of that trend— transition.

Ensuring timely, consistent, and equitable access to the VA services is not just a policy issue, it's a matter of responsibilities. And knowing that we have the full trust and support of our representatives is essential to helping make that transition. Veterans should not have to struggle to receive the care they need after a lifetime of service. And I say lifetime because if you were in Iraq for 2 years or Vietnam for a year, it's a lifetime of service. Thank you.

Uh, Joe, I have 2 quick questions for you before we go to the other panelists. Uh, I appreciate your testimony today, and you, you have such a unique perspective having served alongside both pre-9/11 and post-9/11 veterans. From your perspective, what's the biggest difference in the challenges they face when they come home?

So, um, definitely some of the same things. I'd say post-Gulf War, the Gulf War veterans got little credit for doing anything because the media portrayed it as this bloodless, easygoing— we dropped a few laser bombs and everybody surrendered. And I could tell you that was not the case.

Maybe some units, as in any combat —deployment or any deployment and individuals— some people maybe didn't do anything. Some people were in Riyadh the whole time driving a bus, which I literally know a guy who did that. Important job. I said, there's— all jobs are important. I was in a reconnaissance unit that was up along the Kuwaiti border, months so far north we were out of the artillery fan, meaning we had no support. So when we did get attacked and we were counter with another Iraqi counter-reconnaissance unit, you know, it was tough. So you came home and we didn't get any credit at all. I mean, there were even sometimes at the VA hospital where we were kind of rejected a little bit. Post-9/11, there was an initial response of open arms, right? But then as the war dragged on, and as all wars that last a long time become political, right? It's, oh yeah, you guys did a great job, but you know, look who you're fighting for. I mean, and, and I'm explaining it wrong, but so I say some of the struggles are being accepted as a veteran, right? And, and having other people say, hey, look at it, this is hard and there's a lot of sacrifice. And I

think that one of the things that people don't understand about the last 20-plus years, only 1% of the population served, right? So I have friends of mine that just wrapped up their 25-year career, and I have a friend of mine, I was in the Marines with him, he then worked with us in the State Department and other agencies, went into Army Special Forces, spent 21 years there, and was deployed 16 of 21 years. And he comes home and really nobody wants to deal with, with, with you. Um, and once again, like I said, it's, it's open arms from some folks, complete rejection from other folks, and the struggle at the VA. And I wanna make it clear, a lot of people that work— that I've dealt with at the VA centers, a hospital themselves, they greet you well and they try to help you out. It's when it elevates to that is the problem. I've literally been told, well, you were in the first Gulf War, Joe, that wasn't a real war. I mean, I was literally told that one time. And then another time I was told, um, well, you make enough money and you work, what do you need benefits for?

I said, I'm not even necessarily want benefits, I want my treatment. I was hurt in the Marines and I want the military to continue my treatment, which I have circumstances now that I'm trying to get fixed, and it's just, you know, you're rejected from it. So I don't know if it's the same, if that answered the quest— question or not, but it's kind of— there's a lot of— this stuff is not yes and no.

Let me, uh, end with this, uh, given your experience in both government and the private sector, what's one practical thing New York City could do right now that you think would make a real difference to post-9/11 veterans?

Um, so I think we can take a lesson. I love New York. I may live across the river now, right? But I will say, uh, New York— and I've argued with people literally around the world with this— it's the greatest place in the world, right? But when you go to other states like Florida, or I lived in Texas for a while for work, they let you know everything that's available to you, and they proactively try to help you out. For Texas example, if you're a Texas resident, not like I went there to work and I'm a veteran and I moved there. If you're

a Texas citizen, as they say, right, a state, and you go there and you— I don't remember if you were a combat veteran, I think it was— any state school is free, 100%. This is outside of your VA stuff, right? So if I want to go to A&M, right, it's free. If I want to go— I think Louisiana has a similar thing— if I want to go to LSU— they pay most of the bill. They pick it up. I went, I served, I deployed. It's on them. And this is outside of your GI Bill. So I think New York needs to, as you said before, uh, uh, you know, we need to reallocate some funds. Everybody wants their stuff funded, but when 99% of the population of the United States is leaning on the 1%, and they've been leaning on the 1% for over 20 years— in fact, after the withdrawal from Afghanistan, the enlistment rate dropped to 0.5%. And, and I know a lot of people don't want to acknowledge this right now. And like I said, this comes— you like the President, you don't like the President, you like the Mayor, you like the City Council, you don't— it doesn't matter. These people, veterans, Vietnam veterans— you know, everyone forgets a lot of Vietnam veterans volunteered to go.

They made the call, right? And think about that. 99% of the population does not serve or has no intention of serving, doesn't go in the military. 1% serves. So I would say we could take an example from places like Florida and Texas and proactively say, hey, if you served and— or you're a combat veteran or whatever the case is, CUNY's free. It used to be that way. So if we can find money for all these other special things, you can find money for the 1% of the people who make a lifetime commitment because it doesn't end. And any veteran in here will tell you it doesn't end, right? You deployed once, you're in the military for 2 years, it is with you the rest of your life.
Uh, thank you, Joe, for your service and for your testimony. And I'll just state for the record that everybody knows there's no one that dislikes the City Council. Let's be very clear.
I adore the City Council. I tried to get back into it, but, you know, it is what it is.
I wanna to welcome, uh, wanna welcome, uh, Jenny, uh, Bucove, who is with Gallup NYC and, uh, comes from Howard Beach.

Uh, good morning, Council Members and Chair. Um, I'm Jenny Bucove. I'm the Executive Director of Gallup NYC, and we're New York City's largest therapeutic equine-based nonprofit, and we're based in Queens. At its core, Gallup NYC exists to provide accessible therapeutic experiences with horses for all New Yorkers and we have people come to us from all 5 boroughs. This includes people with physical, cognitive, and emotional challenges. And for many of our riders, this is the first time they've been near a horse, let alone ridden one. And it's often the only way that they would be able to have that access through us. Each week we serve over 400 New Yorkers, including approximately 40 veterans and their family members, I'm proud to say, through riding and unmounted programs. And we're also joined by 100 volunteers each week who support this work. Everyone that comes to us receives a subsidy. Nobody is turned away because of cost. Our veterans programs provide hand-on horse care and riding instruction and opportunities to build connection and community in a setting that feels

comfortable and non-clinical and fun, frankly. We partner directly with the VA New York Harbor Health Care Systems, serving veterans from both the St. Albans and Brooklyn campuses each month. And we are expanding our work through the Veterans Family Program that was initially funded through Dwyer. Thank you for that. Um, which brings veterans and their children together in a fun program which strengthens the ties in the families, rebuilds connections, but also provides a community of people and families that have gone through similar experiences. And we're currently working with, um, the group at Columbia University that developed the Man O' War protocol for PTSD treatment, and we're pulling their best practices into our curriculum as well. As one participant shared, as a veteran with no prior horse experience, Gallop NYC restored a sense of camaraderie that was missing from civilian life. The relationships with the horses and instructors have been a powerful source of healing for my anxiety, depression, and trauma-related challenges. And we're requesting your support in several areas. $150,000 in DVS funding to sustain and expand our

veterans programs, which we are provided free to all participants. Demand continues to grow, particularly as we work more closely with the VA partnerships. Secondly, we are asking for capital funding for an indoor arena, including $250,000 from the Council as part of a broader funding— public funding request. Our programs are canceled when it's snowing, it's raining, or too hot, which is really difficult for our families. It interrupts our services. Um, and by building this indoor arena, it will allow us to build an indoor arena that will ensure consistency. Gallup NYC is a cost-effective, high-impact model that improves mental health, strengthens family, and expands access to care outside of traditional clinical settings. Thank you very much for your support and for the opportunity to testify.
And, um, is there a location for that indoor arena as of yet?
Yes, there is. It's at our, at Sunrise in, at our facility in Queens.

And, uh, obviously Gallup NYC seems like it's doing really unique work with veterans. From what you've seen so far, what

specific outcomes, if any, are you seeing for post-9/11 veterans, and how can the city help scale that impact?

What we find at Gallup is that our— working with us helps people that traditional therapies don't often help, sometimes can't reach. So an obvious one for veterans is PTSD. And so when you come and talk to some of our veterans, they'll tell you that they were very— and we see it, and it's one of the reasons that we've been so successful for the, with the VA, because they see the results that some people come to us and they're very closed off and working with us and working with our horses in particular really opens them up in a way that other therapies don't. That's just one example.
Um, and also with Gallup NYC, we're lucky enough to be joined by Christina Brown Fisher. Go ahead.

Thank you, Chair, and thank you, City Council members. My name is Christina Brown Fisher. I appreciate the opportunity to speak today on behalf of Gallup NYC and the veterans it serves.

When you walk into the Manhattan campus of the Department of Veteran Affairs New York Harbor Health Care System on 23rd Street and 1st Avenue, there's a quote on the wall from George Washington that says, the willingness with which our young people are likely to serve in any war shall be directly proportional to how they perceive the veterans of earlier wars were treated and appreciated by their nation. I am one of those veterans. I served 4 years on active duty in the Air Force. I was an information specialist, and I made a successful transition to television news. I am an Emmy Award-winning journalist, a former anchor and correspondent for MSNBC and NBC News. My work has appeared in The New York Times, HuffPost, and other publications. But my journey with horses did not begin as recreation. It began during neurorehabilitation at a VA medical center in Virginia. Riding was introduced as part of my recovery, and what started as therapy became something much more. It became a path back to myself. When I first began riding, I needed both a side walker and a lead walker just to stay balanced, just

to stay safe. I proudly ride independently now. That's because of Gallup NYC. That progress didn't just happen physically. It rebuilt confidence, independence, and a sense of self that had been shaken. My son began riding at Gallup NYC in 2021. It's become something we share, something that strengthens our connection in a way that's hard to replicate elsewhere. And while I have gained independence, my 8-year-old, who requires significant support, always finds it at Gallup. Sometimes that support looks like riding, but other times it's groundwork. It's learning how to tack, how to groom, and how to feed the horses. Those moments matter just as much. There are lessons being learned both in and out of the saddle, lessons such as patience, responsibility, trust, and confidence that simply cannot be replicated in any traditional setting. There is something uniquely powerful about being around these animals, they demand presence. They respond to calm and consistency. And for veterans, especially those dealing with trauma, injury, or the invisible wounds of service, that environment creates
